subject: chemistry
title: Percentage yield and atom economy
key_idea: Percentage yield compares the product you actually get with the most you could get. Atom economy compares the mass of the desired product with the mass of all the products. A high atom economy wastes less and is better for sustainability.

blocks.text: No reaction gives all of the product it theoretically could. Percentage yield measures how close you got.

items.meaning: The maximum mass of product, calculated from the equation and the limiting reagent.
The mass of product actually obtained.

blocks.label: Percentage yield
where: Both yields in the same unit, either grams or moles.

items.text: 5.00 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH (M = 46.0), makes ethanoic acid: n = 5.00 ÷ 46.0 = 0.109 mol.

items: A yield below 100% is normal. Reasons include an incomplete reaction, side reactions, and product lost in transfers, filtering and purification.
A yield over 100% means the product is impure, often still wet or contaminated with a reactant.
Do a yield calculation from a limiting reagent, not from an excess one.
Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Find the theoretical yield from the limiting reagent.
Yield cannot sensibly exceed 100%.

blocks.text: Atom economy measures how much of the reactant mass ends up in the product you want. It does not depend on how well the experiment is done.

blocks.label: Percentage atom economy
blocks.formula: atom economy = (molar mass of desired product ÷ sum of molar masses of all reactants) × 100
where: Use the coefficients from the balanced equation.
Total reactant mass equals total product mass, so the sum of all products gives the same answer.

items: Atom economy comes from the equation alone.
A reaction can have a high yield and a low atom economy.
Addition reactions have 100% atom economy.

sections.heading: Why a high atom economy matters

blocks.text: A process with a high atom economy turns more of its reactants into useful product. This section covers the benefits for industry and society.

items: **Less waste** by-product, which saves the cost of disposal and cuts pollution.
**Less raw material** used per tonne of product, so finite resources last longer.
**Lower costs** for industry, because fewer reactants are bought and wasted.
Less energy is needed to separate the product from the by-products.
A by-product that has a use can be sold, which means less is thrown away.
Used widely in the chemical industry when choosing between routes to the same product, for example addition reactions and processes that recycle reagents.
High atom economy means less waste and less raw material.
It saves cost and is better for the environment.
Industry compares routes by atom economy.

checks.q: State the difference between percentage yield and atom economy.
checks.a: Percentage yield compares the actual mass of product with the theoretical maximum. Atom economy compares the mass of the desired product with the total mass of reactants (from the equation).

checks.q: Calculate the atom economy for making hydrogen by Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. (M: Fe 55.8, HCl 36.5, H₂ 2.0.)
A student expects 8.40 g of product but obtains 6.72 g. Calculate the percentage yield and give one reason it is below 100%.
checks.a: (6.72 ÷ 8.40) × 100 = 80.0%. Reason: product lost during filtering or transfer, a side reaction, or an incomplete reaction.

items: Calculate percentage yield or related quantities, such as the mass of reactant needed to make a given mass of product.
Link a high atom economy to sustainability in the chemical industry and other areas.

This course writes atom economy as (molar mass of the desired product ÷ sum of the molar masses of all products) × 100%. The sum of the products equals the sum of the reactants when the equation is balanced, so the result is the same.
Know the atom economy formula: (molecular mass of desired product ÷ sum of molecular masses of all reactants) × 100.
Describe the economic, ethical and environmental advantages for society and industry of processes with a high atom economy.
Economic: less waste to treat and lower raw material costs. Ethical and environmental: fewer harmful by-products and less use of finite resources.
